etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Anglo-Norman pretendre, Middle French pretendre (French prétendre (“to claim, demand”)), from Latin praetendere (“to put forward, hold out, pretend”), from prae- (“pre-”) + tendō (“stretch”); see tend.

quote.citation: 1814 May 9, [Jane Austen], chapter VI, in Mansfield Park: […], volume I, London:  […]  [George Sidney] for T[homas] Egerton, […], →OCLC, pages 111–112:
quote.text: "The truth is, Ma'am," said Mrs. Grant, pretending to whisper across the table to Mrs. Norris, "that Dr. Grant hardly knows what the natural taste of our apricot is; […]."

quote.citation: 2003 January 23, Duncan Campbell, The Guardian, London:
quote.text: Luster claimed that the women had consented to sex and were only pretending to be asleep.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To feign, affect (a state, quality, etc.). [from 15th c.]

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book V”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: This let him know, / Lest, wilfully transgressing, he pretend / Surprisal.

Gap and other clothes manufacturers should stop using small subcontractors because they are difficult to control. Instead, they should open up their own fully-owned production facilities so that they cannot pretend ignorance when abuses are committed.

definitions.definition: (intransitive or with 'that' clause or 'to' infinitive) To speak or behave so as to give a false or simulated appearance. [from 14th c.]

quote.citation: 1749, Henry Fielding, chapter 23, in The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling, volume (please specify |volume=I to VI), London: A[ndrew] Millar, […], →OCLC, book XVIII:
quote.text: "After what past at Upton, so soon to engage in a new amour with another woman, while I fancied, and you pretended, your heart was bleeding for me!"

quote.citation: 1963, Margery Allingham, chapter 5, in The China Governess: A Mystery, London: Chatto & Windus, →OCLC:
quote.text: It's rather like a beautiful Inverness cloak one has inherited. Much too good to hide away, so one wears it instead of an overcoat and pretends it's an amusing new fashion.
But I love you / More than I wanted to / There's no point in trying to pretend
I have nothing but contempt for people who hire ghost-writers. But at least most faux authors have the decency to pretend that they are sweating blood over "their" book.

definitions.definition: (intransitive with 'to', formal, originally transitive) To lay claim (to an ability, status, advantage, etc.). [from 15th c.]

quote.text: Chiefs shall be grudged the part which they pretend.

quote.citation: 1946, Bertrand Russell, History of Western Philosophy, I.25:
quote.text: People observed the diversity of schools and the acerbity of their disputes, and decided that all alike were pretending to knowledge which was in fact unattainable.

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To hold before, or put forward, as a cloak or disguise for something else; to exhibit as a veil for something hidden.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book IX”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: Lest that too heavenly form, pretended / To hellish falsehood, snare them.

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To intend; to design, to plot; to attempt.

quote.citation: 1591 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The First Part of Henry the Sixt”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene i]:
quote.text: Such as shall pretend / Malicious practices against his state.

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To hold before one; to extend.

quote.citation: 1596, Edmund Spenser, “Book VI, Canto XI”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: Pastorella  […]  Was by the Captaine all this while defended, / Who, minding more her safety then himselfe, / His target alwayes over her pretended […].

quote.citation: 1596, Edm[und] Spenser, “An Hymne of Heavenly Beautie”, in Fowre Hymnes, London:  […]  [Richard Field] for William Ponsonby, →OCLC, page 43:
quote.text: But had thoſe vvits the vvonders of their dayes, / Or that ſvveete Teian Poet [Anacreon] vvhich did ſpend / His plenteous vaine in ſetting forth her [Venus's] prayſe, / Seene but a glims of this, vvhich I pretend, / Hovv vvondrouſly vvould he her face commend,  […]

definitions.definition: Not really what it is represented as being; imaginary, feigned.
(childish, informal) The act of engaging in pretend play.
